The Indelible Truth: Why Criminal Convictions Must Remain Permanently Public for the Sake of Society

The modern push for expungement and record sealing, often framed as a compassionate step toward "second chances," is fundamentally misguided and dangerously naive. While the impulse to allow individuals to move forward after serving their sentences is understandable, the permanent erasure or concealment of criminal convictions from public view represents a profound betrayal of public safety, victim rights, and the very integrity of our justice system. All criminal convictions must remain permanently and universally accessible to the public without exception. To do otherwise is to prioritize the comfort of the offender over the safety and informed consent of the entire community, undermining the foundational principles of justice, transparency, and collective security.

The most compelling and non-negotiable argument for permanent public access is the paramount right of the public to know and protect themselves. Criminal convictions are not abstract bureaucratic entries; they are factual records of proven harmful conduct that pose real, ongoing risks. When a person is convicted of fraud, embezzlement, or securities violations, employers, investors, and financial institutions have an absolute right to know this history before entrusting them with money or sensitive data. When someone is convicted of assault, domestic violence, or sexual offenses, neighbors, potential romantic partners, parents considering a babysitter, and employers in childcare or eldercare need this information to make informed decisions about safety. Expungement or sealing creates dangerous blind spots. A landlord who unknowingly rents to a serial trespasser because their record was sealed isn't just inconvenienced; they and their other tenants become potential victims. A school district hiring a teacher with a sealed history of child endangerment isn't just making a poor choice; it's placing children directly in harm's way. Secrecy is the ally of reoffending; transparency is the shield of prevention. Pretending a crime never happened because the state papered it over does not magically erase the propensity or history that led to the conviction. Society has a moral and practical obligation to be armed with complete information to assess risk in every interaction where safety or trust is paramount. Denying this information is not compassion; it is institutionalized negligence.

Furthermore, expungement and sealing perpetrate a profound injustice upon victims and their families, effectively silencing their trauma and denying the enduring reality of the harm inflicted. A conviction is the legal acknowledgment of the victim's suffering and the societal condemnation of the act. Sealing or expunging that record sends a devastating message: your pain is no longer relevant; the official record can pretend this never happened. For victims of violent crime, sexual assault, or fraud, the knowledge that the perpetrator could successfully hide their history creates a secondary victimization – a constant, justified fear that the person who caused them immense harm could reintegrate into society without any warning to potential new targets. It denies victims the ongoing validation that the system recognizes the truth of what was done to them. Justice does not conclude with the offender's sentence; it demands enduring accountability visible to the community the offender seeks to rejoin. Permanently hiding the conviction severs the vital link between the crime, its consequences, and the offender's present standing, effectively erasing the victim's experience from the public record and diminishing the societal understanding of the harm caused. Compassion for the victim requires that the truth of the conviction remains accessible so that the community can remain vigilant and the victim's experience is not perpetually invalidated by administrative erasure.

Critics will inevitably invoke "rehabilitation" as the justification for expungement, arguing that permanent records create insurmountable barriers to employment, housing, and reintegration, thereby causing recidivism. This argument is not only flawed but dangerously counterproductive. True rehabilitation is not achieved through deception, but through demonstrable, sustained change in the open. The goal should not be to hide the past but to empower individuals to overcome it while the past is known. If an employer, landlord, or community member sees a conviction but also sees years of spotless conduct, steady employment, community service, and genuine remorse, that is a powerful testament to rehabilitation. Hiding the conviction does not foster genuine reintegration; it fosters dependency on secrecy. It encourages offenders to present a sanitized, false narrative rather than taking full responsibility and proving their change through transparent action. Moreover, expungement creates a perverse incentive: offenders may focus energy on getting their record cleared legally rather than on the hard, ongoing work of internal change. It also fosters distrust – if a hidden record surfaces later (as they often do through non-public channels or new offenses), the damage to the offender's credibility is catastrophic, potentially destroying the very reintegration expungement promised. Real opportunity comes when society can see and verify sustained positive change, not when the past is magically erased. Permanently accessible records allow for nuanced judgment – focusing on recent behavior, evidence of rehabilitation, and the nature of the offense – rather than the false binary of "clean record" vs. "tainted record" that expungement creates.

The integrity of the justice system itself is critically undermined by expungement and sealing. Convictions are the result of rigorous (though imperfect) legal processes: arrest, probable cause, indictment, trial (or plea), sentencing by a judge or jury. These outcomes are not mere "allegations"; they represent society's formal, adjudicated finding of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. To later declare such a finding "null and void" for public purposes, or to shroud it in secrecy, fundamentally misrepresents the outcome of that process. It creates a bizarre legal fiction: "This person was found guilty by the highest standards of our law, but now, for convenience, we will pretend it never happened." This erodes public trust in the seriousness of convictions and the finality of justice. If convictions can be made to disappear, what does that say about the gravity of the process that produced them? It suggests the system itself is uncertain of its own conclusions. Furthermore, selective expungement inevitably leads to inequity and abuse. If exceptions are made (for "minor" crimes, or after a certain time), it creates arbitrary distinctions that disproportionately benefit those with resources to navigate the complex expungement process, often leaving the poor and marginalized – the very groups proponents claim to help – unable to access the "clean slate." True reform must focus on preventing unjust convictions and ensuring fair sentencing at the front end, not on hiding the outcomes at the back end. The solution to a biased system isn't to erase the evidence of bias; it's to fix the bias itself. Keeping records public provides essential data for identifying and combating systemic inequities in policing and prosecution.

Finally, the argument for permanent access is rooted in the bedrock principle of a transparent and accountable society. Democracies thrive on information. Citizens have a right to know about the conduct of others within the community, especially conduct proven to threaten safety or violate fundamental laws. Criminal records are not private diaries; they are public adjudications resulting from the state's exercise of its power to maintain order. Concealing them privatizes public justice, turning societal safety into a game of hidden information and luck. It forces individuals to rely on unreliable rumors, private investigators, or invasive background checks that often surface inaccurate information, rather than providing a single, official, and truthful public record. Permanent public access is the most equitable, transparent, and ultimately safest system possible. It allows everyone – employers, landlords, neighbors, potential victims – to make decisions based on the complete factual picture, fostering a community where trust is earned through visible, sustained good conduct, not through the disappearance of past wrongs.

The call for expungement and sealing is seductive in its promise of a fresh start, but it is a promise built on sand – a promise that sacrifices concrete, provable safety for an illusion of redemption built on secrecy. Victims deserve the enduring validation of the truth. The public deserves unobstructed access to information critical for its protection. Society deserves a justice system whose outcomes are respected and transparent, not selectively erased. Rehabilitation is proven through action in the light of day, not through hiding in the shadows of a sealed record. To permanently prohibit the expungement or sealing of any criminal conviction is not to be cruel; it is to be ruthlessly committed to truth, accountability, and the unwavering protection of the innocent. It is the only policy that honestly serves the long-term safety and integrity of our communities. Let the record stand, indelible and public, not as a mark of eternal shame, but as an enduring beacon of truth in the service of a safer, more just, and ultimately more trustworthy society. Anything less is a dangerous gamble with the security and well-being of us all.

From a perspective prioritizing public safety and transparency as paramount values, the maintenance of permanent, publicly accessible criminal conviction records without expungement is argued to be essential for the following reasons and supposed benefits:

Core Rationale: Public Safety as the Non-Negotiable Priority

This viewpoint holds that society's collective safety must supersede individual rehabilitation goals. Criminal history is seen as a permanent and predictive indicator of future risk, especially for certain offenses. Removing records is viewed as recklessly obscuring vital risk information.

Key Reasons & Supposed Benefits

  1. Maximizing Informed Risk Assessment by the Public:

    • Reason: The public (employers, landlords, educators, parents, neighbors, romantic partners) has a fundamental right and need to know about an individual's past criminal conduct to make informed safety decisions.
    • Benefits: Prevents vulnerable populations (e.g., children, tenants, employees) from unknowingly being exposed to potential harm. Enables landlords to screen for violent offenders, employers in sensitive roles (childcare, finance, security) to assess suitability, and individuals to make safer personal choices. Expungement is seen as creating "hidden risks" that could lead to preventable victimization.

  2. Deterrence and Ongoing Accountability:

    • Reason: The certainty of permanent public consequences serves as a powerful deterrent both for initial offending and, crucially, for recidivism. Knowing a conviction will permanently follow them creates a continuous incentive for law-abiding behavior post-release.
    • Benefits: Strengthens the perceived seriousness of the criminal justice system. Undermines the argument that "time served" is the only consequence; permanent record acts as a lifelong incentive for compliance. Expungement is viewed as prematurely removing this critical behavioral deterrent, potentially increasing the likelihood of re-offending.

  3. Preventing Concealment of Dangerous Histories:

    • Reason: Expungement allows individuals with histories of serious violence, sexual offenses, fraud, or repeat offenses to legally conceal their past. This is seen as enabling predators, violent individuals, or chronic offenders to hide in plain sight.
    • Benefits: Ensures that patterns of criminal behavior (e.g., serial domestic violence, financial fraud, sexual misconduct) remain visible for identification and monitoring. Critical for community notification systems (like sex offender registries, which often operate alongside but independently of public records) and for law enforcement tracking potential threats. Eliminating access creates "blind spots" for those responsible for public safety.

  4. Preserving Data Integrity and Transparency in the Justice System:

    • Reason: Permanent public records are vital for independent oversight of law enforcement, prosecution, and judicial decision-making. They allow researchers, journalists, and watchdog groups to analyze patterns (e.g., racial disparities, charging practices, sentencing trends) without the distortion caused by expunged data.
    • Benefits: Fosters accountability within the justice system itself. Enables evidence-based policy analysis (e.g., evaluating the effectiveness of specific laws or programs by studying actual outcomes, not artificially sanitized data). Expungement is seen as erasing historical truth and hindering efforts to improve systemic fairness through data.

  5. Protecting Victims' Rights and Societal Recognition of Harm:

    • Reason: Crimes inflict harm on victims and society. Permanent records serve as an enduring acknowledgment of that harm and the resulting societal judgment. Expungement is interpreted as erasing the victim's experience and the societal consequence of the offense.
    • Benefits: Validates victims' experiences and provides a permanent factual account of the crime. Prevents offenders from effectively "rewriting history" and presenting themselves as never having committed a serious offense, which can be particularly distressing for victims of violent crimes.

  6. Ensuring Consistency in Risk Assessment Across Jurisdictions:

    • Reason: Expungement laws vary wildly by state (or even county). An offense expunged in one jurisdiction might not be recognized elsewhere, creating inconsistent and unreliable risk profiles.
    • Benefits: A universally permanent national (or state-level) record system provides consistent data for background checks conducted anywhere, crucial for roles requiring multi-state mobility (e.g., commercial driving, certain healthcare licenses). Expungement creates patchwork reliability that undermines national security and safety in mobile professions.

  7. Upholding the Principle of "Truth in Sentencing" Beyond Incarceration:

    • Reason: Sentencing isn't solely about time served; it includes the lasting consequences of the conviction (collateral consequences like loss of voting rights, certain licenses, etc.). Expungement is viewed as contradicting the original court judgment and artificially mitigating consequences the system deemed necessary for public protection.
    • Benefits: Maintains the integrity of the judicial finding of guilt. Reflects that some acts are so harmful (e.g., murder, rape, serious child abuse) that society has a perpetual right to know, regardless of time elapsed. Prioritizes the gravity of the offense over the offender's subsequent behavior.

Viewpoint on Rehabilitation Concerns

Proponents of this stance explicitly reject the primacy of rehabilitation arguments in this context:

  • Safety Trumps Second Chances: They argue that society's right to safety is inviolable. Granting a "clean slate" through expungement is portrayed as sacrificing potential future victims on the altar of an offender's convenience.
  • Rehabilitation is Demonstrated, Not Granted: They contend that true rehabilitation is proven through sustained law-abiding behavior over a very long period, but this should inform risk assessment (e.g., older, minor offenses might be weighted less by a prudent landlord), not erase the factual history. The record itself doesn't prevent employment/housing; poor judgment in using the record does – and they argue the law shouldn't restrict access to protect offenders from that judgment.
  • "Fresh Start" is Available Through Behavior: They assert that individuals can rebuild lives despite the record by demonstrating decades of lawful conduct; the record merely provides context for others to evaluate that claim. Removing the record is seen as granting an unearned advantage, not a necessary tool for success.
  • Risk is Unknowable: They argue that recidivism risk, especially for certain crimes (violent, sexual), can never be reliably predicted to be zero. Permanent records are the only way to manage this inherent uncertainty for public protection.

Conclusion from This Viewpoint

Maintaining permanent, public access to criminal conviction records is seen as a non-negotiable safeguard for a free society. It is fundamentally about empowering the public with knowledge to protect themselves, ensuring the justice system's actions remain transparent and accountable, upholding the seriousness of criminal offenses, and prioritizing the prevention of future victimization above all else. Expungement, in this framework, is viewed as a dangerous experiment that trades concrete, tangible public safety benefits for an unproven and secondary goal (easier reintegration), potentially at the cost of future innocent lives. The "presumption of ongoing risk" associated with certain convictions is deemed a necessary and rational basis for permanent transparency.

The Case for Permanent Public Access to Criminal Records

Introduction

I'll present the strongest arguments for this position, while noting upfront that this is a contentious issue with significant countervailing considerations.

Arguments for Permanent Public Accessibility

Public Safety and Informed Decision-Making

The most compelling argument centers on community protection. Employers, landlords, schools, and volunteer organizations make daily decisions that affect vulnerable populations. Permanent record accessibility ensures:

  • Childcare providers can screen employees for offenses against minors
  • Financial institutions can identify applicants with fraud convictions
  • Housing complexes can assess applicants with violent crime histories
  • Businesses can evaluate trustworthiness for positions involving access to finances or sensitive information

Without complete records, decision-makers operate with incomplete information, potentially placing others at risk.

Accountability and Deterrence

Permanent consequences reinforce the gravity of criminal behavior. When individuals understand that convictions carry lasting reputational effects, this may:

  • Strengthen deterrent effects beyond incarceration alone
  • Emphasize personal responsibility for one's actions
  • Maintain respect for the criminal justice system's authority

Consistency and Equal Treatment

Expungement creates a two-tiered system where:

  • Those who can afford lawyers obtain fresh starts
  • Those without resources carry permanent marks
  • Outcomes depend on legal sophistication rather than rehabilitation

Universal accessibility eliminates this disparity—everyone faces identical consequences regardless of wealth or legal representation.

Victim Considerations

Crime victims often express that expungement minimizes their suffering. Permanent records:

  • Validate victims' experiences by maintaining official acknowledgment
  • Prevent offenders from presenting falsified histories
  • Allow victims to verify an offender's status when safety concerns arise

Protection of Record Integrity

Criminal records constitute historical fact. Allowing alteration:

  • Compromises the accuracy of judicial records
  • Creates opportunities for selective memory and revisionist history
  • Undermines the integrity of public documentation systems

Technological Realities

In the internet age, information rarely disappears completely. Expungement creates legal fiction—records may be "sealed" officially while remaining accessible through:

  • News archives
  • Social media posts
  • Private background check companies
  • Internet searches

This disconnect between legal status and practical reality means expungement often provides false hope rather than genuine relief.

Counterarguments Worth Considering

Rehabilitation and Redemption: Critics argue permanent accessibility undermines rehabilitation by creating perpetual punishment. Research shows employment barriers increase recidivism rates, suggesting some pathway to record limitation might serve public safety better than permanent accessibility.

Youthful Offenses: Brain development research indicates adolescents have diminished culpability. Permanent records for juvenile offenses may be disproportionate.

Criminal Justice Errors: Wrongful convictions occur. Even with appeals processes, some argue those who complete sentences shouldn't face lifetime consequences for potentially flawed adjudications.

Minor Offenses: The criminal code criminalizes behaviors ranging from serious violence to technical violations. Permanent accessibility for all offenses treats vastly different conduct identically.

Racial and Economic Disparities: Given documented disparities in arrests, prosecutions, and convictions, permanent record accessibility may entrench systemic inequalities.

Conclusion

The strongest case for permanent public accessibility rests on prioritizing community safety, maintaining accountability, and ensuring informed decision-making. These arguments deserve serious consideration in policy debates.

However, absolute positions rarely produce optimal policy. The most thoughtful approach might involve:

  • Maintaining accessibility for serious violent and sexual offenses
  • Creating pathways for sealing certain minor offenses after substantial time
  • Improving record accuracy and context
  • Addressing underlying disparities in the criminal justice system

The Case for Permanent Public Criminal Records: Why Transparency Must Trump Expungement

Introduction

In an era where information accessibility has become paramount to public safety and informed decision-making, the practice of expunging or sealing criminal records represents a dangerous step backward. While advocates of record expungement frame their position around second chances and rehabilitation, the permanent maintenance of public criminal records serves far more critical societal functions: protecting vulnerable populations, ensuring accountability, preserving the integrity of our justice system, and upholding the public's fundamental right to information. Criminal convictions, regardless of their nature or age, should remain permanently accessible to the public without exception.

The Imperative of Public Safety

The primary obligation of any society is to protect its citizens from harm. Criminal records serve as an essential tool in this protective framework. When employers, landlords, or community organizations can access complete criminal histories, they make informed decisions that safeguard those under their care. Consider the daycare operator screening potential employees, the elderly homeowner hiring a caregiver, or the youth sports league vetting volunteer coaches. These scenarios demand complete transparency about an individual's criminal past.

Expungement creates dangerous blind spots in our safety net. A person with a sealed conviction for child endangerment could theoretically work in a school, while someone with an expunged fraud conviction might handle financial transactions for vulnerable seniors. The argument that people deserve second chances cannot supersede the right of potential victims to be protected from known risks. Statistical evidence demonstrates that while many offenders do not reoffend, recidivism rates remain significant enough across all crime categories to justify continued vigilance. The public has a right to make informed decisions about whom they trust with their safety, their children, and their property.

Preserving Judicial Accountability and Preventing Manipulation

Public criminal records serve as a crucial check on judicial power and ensure the accountability of our legal system. When records can be sealed or expunged, it becomes impossible for journalists, researchers, and watchdog organizations to monitor patterns in prosecution, sentencing disparities, or judicial misconduct. This transparency is fundamental to maintaining public trust in our institutions.

Furthermore, the expungement process itself is susceptible to corruption and inequality. Wealthy defendants with access to superior legal representation are disproportionately successful in having their records cleared, while indigent offenders often lack the resources or knowledge to pursue expungement. This creates a two-tiered system where justice becomes contingent on economic status rather than actual rehabilitation or merit. The permanent maintenance of public records ensures that all individuals, regardless of their socioeconomic status, face equal and lasting consequences for their criminal actions.

History provides numerous examples of attempts to manipulate or destroy criminal records for political purposes or to protect powerful individuals. Only through permanent, publicly accessible records can we prevent such abuses and ensure that the historical record remains intact for future generations to study and learn from.

The Fundamental Right to Information

In a democratic society, citizens possess an inherent right to access information about legal proceedings and their outcomes. Criminal trials are public proceedings precisely because justice must not only be done but be seen to be done. The conviction that results from these public proceedings should similarly remain in the public domain. To seal or expunge these records is to retroactively deny the public's right to know about events that occurred in open court.

This principle extends beyond individual cases to encompass broader societal interests. Researchers studying crime patterns, journalists investigating systemic issues, and policymakers crafting evidence-based legislation all depend on comprehensive criminal justice data. When records are expunged, these vital functions of democracy are undermined. We cannot address problems we cannot fully see or measure.

Moreover, victims of crimes have a legitimate interest in the permanent documentation of offenses committed against them. Expungement can feel like a denial of their experience and suffering, particularly when they may encounter their attacker in professional or social settings where others are unaware of the person's history. The permanent record serves as a validation of their experience and a warning to other potential victims.

Addressing Counterarguments

Advocates for expungement often argue that permanent records prevent rehabilitation and reintegration into society. However, this argument fails to acknowledge that actions have consequences, and criminal behavior represents a fundamental breach of social trust that cannot simply be erased. Society can support rehabilitation through various means—job training programs, counseling services, graduated re-entry assistance—without resorting to the fiction that crimes never occurred.

The claim that permanent records doom individuals to perpetual unemployment and marginalization is overstated. Many employers already consider the nature and age of convictions in their hiring decisions, and numerous successful individuals have rebuilt their lives despite public criminal records. The solution to employment challenges lies not in hiding information but in educating employers about realistic risk assessment and providing incentives for hiring reformed offenders.

Some argue that minor offenses or crimes committed in youth should be eligible for expungement. Yet this seemingly reasonable position opens the door to subjective determinations about which crimes are "minor" and creates arbitrary distinctions that undermine the principle of equal justice. A shoplifting conviction may seem minor until we consider the small business owner driven to bankruptcy by theft. A juvenile assault may appear less serious until we account for the lasting trauma inflicted on the victim.

The Benefits of Permanent Records in the Digital Age

Modern technology has made the maintenance and accessibility of criminal records more efficient and cost-effective than ever before. Digital databases can provide instant, accurate information while preventing the loss or degradation of paper records. This technological capability should be embraced rather than restricted.

Furthermore, permanent public records facilitate important research into criminal justice outcomes, rehabilitation effectiveness, and societal trends. Longitudinal studies tracking offenders over decades provide invaluable insights that inform policy and practice. Expungement destroys this data, leaving us blind to patterns that could improve our justice system and prevent future crimes.

The digital age also enables nuanced presentation of criminal record information. Rather than simple expungement, technology allows for contextual information to be included with records—time elapsed since conviction, evidence of rehabilitation, completion of sentences—providing a more complete picture while maintaining transparency.

International Perspectives and Precedents

Many nations with lower crime rates than those allowing expungement maintain permanent criminal records, suggesting that record sealing is not necessary for successful rehabilitation or public safety. Countries like Japan and Singapore, known for their low crime rates and successful reintegration programs, maintain comprehensive criminal record systems. Their success demonstrates that rehabilitation and permanent records are not mutually exclusive but can work together in a comprehensive approach to criminal justice.

Conclusion

The proposal to permanently prohibit expungement or sealing of criminal records is not about perpetual punishment but about maintaining the integrity, transparency, and safety of our society. Criminal convictions represent significant events where individuals chose to violate society's laws and caused harm to others. These historical facts cannot and should not be erased simply because time has passed or circumstances have changed.

The permanent maintenance of public criminal records serves multiple crucial functions: protecting potential victims, ensuring judicial accountability, preserving the public's right to information, facilitating research and policy development, and maintaining the historical record. While we must certainly support paths to rehabilitation and reintegration for former offenders, these goals should not come at the expense of public safety and transparency.

In our interconnected society, where trust and information form the foundation of countless daily interactions, we cannot afford to create blind spots in our knowledge about those with whom we interact. The complete and permanent accessibility of criminal records is not merely a policy preference but a fundamental requirement for a safe, transparent, and accountable society. The risks of expungement far outweigh any theoretical benefits, and we must resist efforts to obscure criminal histories that rightfully belong in the public domain. Only through complete transparency can we build a society that is both just and secure for all its members.

Introduction

In an era where transparency and accountability form the bedrock of a just society, the practice of expungement and sealing of criminal records stands as a dangerous aberration. The primary rationale for maintaining permanent public access to criminal records is the protection of public safety. Beyond immediate safety, prohibiting expungement reinforces deterrence and accountability, core pillars of an effective criminal justice system. Criminal behavior thrives in environments where consequences can be easily erased, but permanent records serve as a lifelong reminder of one's actions, discouraging future violations. Criminological research, including a landmark 2015 study in the Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology, demonstrates that the visibility of convictions reduces reoffending by up to 25% through social and psychological mechanisms like shame and reputation loss. Permanently prohibiting the expungement or sealing of criminal records is not merely a policy preference but a moral and practical necessity. By ensuring all convictions remain publicly accessible without exception, society safeguards public safety, bolsters deterrence and accountability, and upholds the right to informed decision-making. In an era increasingly preoccupied with second chances and digital privacy, the notion of permanently prohibiting the expungement or sealing of criminal records may seem harsh. However, the integrity of public safety, the principles of justice, and the rights of victims demand that all criminal convictions remain publicly accessible without exception. Criminal records are not mere administrative files; they are vital repositories of truth that inform societal trust, deter criminal behavior, and safeguard communities. This essay argues that sealing or expunging such records undermines these foundational values and must be permanently prohibited.

Public Safety: A Shield Against Recurring Harm
The primary duty of any society is to protect its citizens, and transparency in criminal records is a cornerstone of this responsibility. When individuals with violent or predatory histories can erase their pasts, they gain unfettered access to positions of trust—such as education, healthcare, and childcare—posing risks to vulnerable populations. For instance, a person with a domestic abuse conviction who becomes a school administrator may exploit their position to perpetuate harm. Background checks, while a tool for screening, are inconsistent: employers may neglect them, and loopholes exist for record-seekers. By maintaining permanent public access, society creates a robust defense mechanism, enabling informed decisions that prioritize safety over the convenience of offenders.

Justice and Accountability: Upholding the Integrity of the Legal System
Justice is not merely about punishment; it is about accountability and transparency. A criminal conviction is a legal judgment, a societal statement that wrongdoing occurred and was addressed. Expungement erases this record, effectively allowing offenders to rewrite their histories and diminishing the significance of their punishment. If a person can "start anew" by vanishing into the crowd, what deterrent remains for future misconduct? Moreover, the public’s right to know is a democratic principle. Just as traffic violations or professional licenses are publicly accessible, criminal records serve as a ledger of individual responsibility. To conceal them is to betray the very essence of a just society.

Protection of Victims: Honoring Their Rights and Safety
Victims of crime deserve more than legal closure; they deserve assurance that offenders remain accountable. Sealing records can retraumatize victims by implying that their suffering is forgettable or inconsequential. For survivors of sexual assault or violent crimes, public registries and accessible records provide a sense of security, enabling communities to protect themselves from potential threats. Consider a neighborhood unaware that a registered sex offender has moved in under a new identity—such scenarios are not hypothetical but preventable through transparency. Public access to records is not merely informational; it is an act of solidarity with victims, affirming that their experiences matter.

Addressing Counterarguments: Balancing Rehabilitation and Accountability
Critics argue that expungement facilitates rehabilitation by allowing offenders to reintegrate into society. Yet true rehabilitation is not about erasing the past but about transforming behavior while remaining answerable for it. The justice system’s role is not to enable oblivion but to enforce consequences. Alternatives to expungement—such as job training, mentorship, and community service—can support reintegration without compromising transparency. Furthermore, in the digital age, the idea that expungement "erases" records is a myth; data often lingers in shadowy corners of the internet. Why, then, should the law pretend to offer a clean slate when the reality is far more complex?

Conclusion
The permanent accessibility of criminal records is not a punitive stance but a necessary safeguard for societal well-being. It fortifies public safety, upholds the dignity of justice, and honors the rights of victims. While compassion for offenders is essential, it must never eclipse the collective need for truth and protection. To permit the sealing or expungement of records is to invite peril and hypocrisy. Let us instead embrace a system where accountability is eternal, and justice is unyielding—a system where the past is never forgotten, and the public is always informed.

Introduction

The concept of expunging or sealing criminal records has become a highly debated topic in contemporary legal and social discourse. Proponents argue that such measures can provide individuals who have served their sentences a chance to reintegrate into society, free from the stigma and obstacles associated with past convictions. However, this essay takes a firm stance against the expungement or sealing of criminal records. It argues that all criminal convictions should remain permanently accessible to the public, without exception. The rationale for this position is grounded in the principles of transparency, public safety, deterrence, and the preservation of justice.

Transparency and Accountability

In a free and democratic society, transparency is a fundamental value that ensures accountability and trust. The permanence of criminal records serves as an essential measure to uphold this transparency. By maintaining comprehensive and accessible records of criminal convictions, citizens are empowered with knowledge about the histories of those in their communities. This informed awareness enables individuals to make educated decisions regarding their personal and professional relationships, as well as engage in meaningful discussions about public policy and criminal justice reform.

Furthermore, the ability to access a person's criminal history fosters accountability on multiple levels. For the convicted individual, the enduring record serves as a reminder of their actions and their responsibility to learn from their mistakes. For law enforcement and the judicial system, unalterable records provide a means to evaluate patterns, identify recidivism risks, and ensure appropriate sentencing, thereby bolstering the efficiency and effectiveness of these institutions.

Public Safety

The paramount obligation of any government is to protect the safety and well-being of its citizens. A crucial aspect of fulfilling this duty lies in the maintenance of accurate and open criminal records. The public's right to know outweighs the desire for an individual's privacy, particularly when it concerns potential threats to the community.

For instance, employers have a responsibility to provide safe environments for their employees and customers. In fields such as education, healthcare, and childcare, access to criminal records is essential to ensuring the hiring of trustworthy and suitable candidates. Moreover, in situations involving housing, adoption, and volunteer work, the disclosure of criminal histories can prevent potentially dangerous situations and safeguard vulnerable populations.

Deterrence and Rehabilitation

The Case Against Expungement: Why Criminal Records Must Remain Public Forever

Introduction

In an era where second chances are often celebrated as fundamental to human dignity, a dangerous misconception has taken root in our criminal justice system: the belief that criminal records should be erased or sealed to allow offenders to move forward. While this perspective appeals to our sense of mercy and redemption, it fundamentally undermines public safety, transparency, and true accountability. This position protects society's most vulnerable members, maintains institutional integrity, and ensures that the consequences of criminal behavior are fully felt and understood.

Public Safety Requires Complete Information

The most compelling argument against expungement lies in its direct threat to public safety. When criminal records disappear from public view, communities lose their ability to make informed decisions about personal and professional interactions. Consider the implications: a registered sex offender whose record was sealed applies for a job in a daycare center, or a violent assault convict moves into a neighborhood unaware to existing residents.

Public access to criminal records serves as a crucial protective mechanism for society's most vulnerable populations—children, elderly individuals, and potential victims of domestic violence. These records provide essential information that allows community members to assess risks and take appropriate precautions. Removing this information creates dangerous blind spots that criminals themselves may not even recognize they're exploiting.

Furthermore, the public nature of criminal records serves as a deterrent to reoffending. When individuals know their actions will be permanently documented and accessible, they may think twice before committing additional crimes. Expungement eliminates this powerful deterrent effect, potentially encouraging recidivism by reducing the perceived consequences of criminal behavior.

Transparency and Government Accountability

Open criminal records represent essential government transparency that citizens deserve and require. When criminal proceedings become sealed or expunged, it creates a dangerous precedent where government institutions can operate in secrecy. Taxpayers fund law enforcement, prosecution, and judicial proceedings with the expectation that these processes remain visible and accountable.

Secret courts and hidden criminal histories undermine democratic principles of open governance. Citizens cannot evaluate the effectiveness of their criminal justice system if they cannot see how it operates. They cannot identify patterns of corruption, bias, or ineffectiveness. They cannot hold public officials accountable for their decisions. Permanently public criminal records ensure that the machinery of justice remains visible and subject to public scrutiny.

Moreover, government agencies responsible for protecting public welfare—such as licensing boards, school districts, and child protective services—require complete criminal histories to fulfill their mandates effectively. When records are sealed, these agencies operate with incomplete information, potentially compromising their ability to protect the public trust.

The Illusion of Redemption Through Erasure

Proponents of expungement argue that it offers opportunities for genuine redemption and rehabilitation. However, this perspective confuses the act of forgiveness with the erasure of consequences. True rehabilitation involves accepting responsibility for one's actions and living with the natural outcomes of those choices—not pretending they never occurred.

Permanent public records serve as constant reminders of the real-world impact of criminal behavior. They force individuals to confront the harm they've caused rather than allowing them to simply start fresh. This ongoing reminder can be a powerful motivator for lawful behavior and genuine personal growth.

Additionally, the process of rebuilding a life despite a public criminal record often builds stronger character than beginning with a clean slate. Individuals learn resilience, accountability, and the value of honest labor when they must overcome documented transgressions. This creates more genuinely rehabilitated citizens than those who escape consequences through legal manipulation.

Economic and Social Fairness

Maintaining public criminal records also promotes economic and social fairness. Employers, landlords, and community organizations have legitimate interests in knowing about applicants' backgrounds, particularly when those positions involve trust, responsibility, or vulnerable populations.

Complete information allows these entities to make informed decisions that protect their interests and those of the communities they serve. A employer hiring someone for a financial position, a landlord renting to families with children, or a volunteer coordinator working with youth all deserve access to complete criminal histories.

When records are expunged, it creates an uneven playing field where some individuals gain unfair advantages through legal technicalities rather than genuine merit. This undermines the principle that success should be earned through honest effort rather than legal maneuvering around documented wrongdoing.

Addressing Counterarguments

Those who support expungement often argue that it provides necessary second chances for people to contribute positively to society. While second chances are indeed valuable, they don't require erasing evidence of past wrongdoing. Society can offer opportunities for redemption while still maintaining transparency about an individual's history.

Others claim that sealed records allow people to overcome stigma and achieve normalcy. However, this perspective prioritizes individual convenience over collective safety. The goal of criminal justice should be protection of society, not comfort for offenders.

Some argue that criminal records create permanent barriers to employment that constitute cruel and unusual punishment. This view fundamentally misunderstands the nature of justice, which necessarily includes proportional consequences for harmful actions. If employment consequences are too severe, the solution lies in revising relevant laws, not in destroying evidence of actual criminal conduct.

Conclusion

Permanently public criminal records represent an essential component of transparent, accountable, and effective criminal justice. They protect vulnerable populations, ensure government accountability, promote genuine rehabilitation, and maintain social fairness. While the desire to offer second chances reflects noble impulses, it cannot justify eliminating evidence of actual criminal conduct.

The path forward lies not in erasing records but in creating better systems for reintegration that acknowledge both past wrongs and present potential. Society can welcome former offenders while still insisting that their criminal histories remain visible. True justice requires both mercy and accountability—and both demands that criminal records remain permanently public.

Only through complete transparency can we build a criminal justice system that truly serves justice, protects the innocent, and creates genuine opportunities for redemption within a framework of honest accountability.

Introduction

The Primacy of Public Safety

At the heart of any civilized society lies the duty to protect its citizens from harm. Permanent public access to criminal records is an indispensable tool in fulfilling this duty. When convictions are expunged or sealed, potential employers, landlords, educators, and even romantic partners are left in the dark about an individual's past behaviors. Consider the case of background checks: according to a 2022 report by the Society for Human Resource Management, 95% of employers conduct criminal background screenings to mitigate risks. If records are hidden, these checks become meaningless, allowing dangerous individuals to infiltrate sensitive environments.

For instance, in states like California and New York, where expungement is liberally granted for non-violent offenses, there have been documented cases of repeat offenders slipping through the cracks. A 2019 study by the RAND Corporation found that individuals with sealed records had a 12% higher recidivism rate in certain categories, partly because the lack of scrutiny reduced external pressures for reform. By contrast, countries like Japan, which maintain stringent public access to criminal histories, report lower rates of repeat offenses in high-risk categories such as sexual crimes. Prohibiting expungement ensures that society can make informed decisions—hiring a reformed thief for a cash-handling job might be acceptable with full disclosure, but sealing that record deceives and endangers. Public safety is not negotiable; it demands unfiltered truth, not sanitized narratives.

Fostering Accountability and Deterrence

Criminal justice is not merely about punishment; it is about accountability that endures beyond a sentence's completion. Allowing expungement or sealing sends a perilous message: crimes can be forgotten, and consequences erased. This erodes personal responsibility, as offenders may view their actions as temporary stains rather than permanent lessons. A permanent record, however, serves as a lifelong reminder, compelling individuals to confront their past and strive for genuine change.

Psychological studies support this: research from the American Psychological Association indicates that visible accountability—such as ongoing public scrutiny—significantly reduces recidivism by reinforcing internal moral compasses. Deterrence theory, pioneered by criminologists like Cesare Beccaria, posits that the certainty and permanence of consequences are more effective than severity alone. If a conviction vanishes after a few years, the deterrent effect diminishes; potential offenders perceive the system as lenient, emboldening them to act. In the United States, where over 70 million adults have criminal records (per the Bureau of Justice Statistics), allowing expungement for even minor offenses creates a revolving door of hidden risks. By mandating perpetual public access, we deter not only the offender but also society at large, signaling that no crime is inconsequential enough to be buried.

Moreover, this approach aligns with ethical imperatives. Hiding records is akin to historical revisionism—erasing facts to suit convenience. Just as we do not expunge war crimes from global memory, we should not seal individual transgressions. Accountability demands visibility; without it, justice becomes a farce.

Upholding Justice for Victims and Ensuring Equality

Victims of crime endure lasting scars, yet expungement trivializes their suffering by allowing offenders to rewrite their stories. A rape survivor, for example, may find no solace in knowing their assailant's record is sealed, effectively denying public acknowledgment of the harm inflicted. Permanent records honor victims by preserving the truth, ensuring that society remembers and learns from atrocities. As victims' rights advocate Marsy's Law emphasizes, transparency is a cornerstone of restorative justice, providing closure and preventing perpetrators from evading societal judgment.

A 2021 ACLU report highlighted racial disparities in expungement approvals, with white offenders 1.5 times more likely to succeed than Black counterparts. By eliminating expungement entirely, we level the playing field: no one, from the white-collar embezzler to the street-level dealer, escapes the shadow of their actions. This universality fosters a fairer society, where consequences are blind to wealth or status. Exceptions breed inequality; permanence ensures equity.

Addressing Counterarguments: Rehabilitation Versus Reality

Opponents of this stance often invoke rehabilitation and second chances, arguing that permanent records stigmatize offenders, hindering employment and reintegration. They claim expungement aids societal reentry, reducing recidivism. However, this perspective is misguided and empirically flawed. True rehabilitation thrives on honesty, not concealment. Privacy concerns also arise, with critics asserting that non-violent offenders deserve a clean slate after time served. Yet, privacy is not absolute; it yields to public interest in matters of safety. Just as we publicly register sex offenders under laws like Megan's Law, all convictions warrant disclosure. Exceptions for "minor" crimes are slippery slopes—what qualifies as minor? A DUI that killed no one today could tomorrow. No: all crimes reflect character flaws that society must know to protect itself. The notion that time heals all records ignores repeat offenders like serial fraudsters who exploit sealed pasts. Rehabilitation is possible with visibility; hiding records merely postpones accountability, inviting relapse.

Finally, the emotional appeal for mercy overlooks the greater good. While empathy for reformed offenders is valid, it must not supersede collective security. Societies that prioritize transparency, like those in Scandinavia with open criminal databases, boast lower crime rates without widespread expungement. We must reject the fallacy that forgiveness requires forgetting.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the permanent prohibition of expungement and sealing criminal records is not an act of vengeance but a safeguard for a just and secure society. By ensuring all convictions remain publicly accessible without exception, we prioritize public safety, enforce accountability, deter future crimes, honor victims, and promote true equality. The evidence—from statistical studies to real-world examples—overwhelmingly supports this position, debunking myths of rehabilitation through obscurity. It is time for policymakers to act decisively: enact laws mandating lifelong public access to criminal records, dismantling the dangerous illusion of erasable sins. Let us build a transparent world where truth prevails, protecting the innocent and holding the guilty eternally accountable. The cost of hidden histories is too high; the benefits of openness are immeasurable. Demand this change—for our communities, our children, and the integrity of justice itself.

Introduction

The criminal justice system serves as the bedrock of societal order, tasked with adjudicating wrongdoing and maintaining public safety. Public Safety and the Right to Know

The primary argument for permanent public access to criminal records is rooted in the fundamental right to public safety. Citizens have a vested interest in knowing the history of those who share their spaces, workplaces, and neighborhoods. When a criminal record is sealed or expunged, it creates a dangerous information asymmetry. A neighbor, a colleague, or a new acquaintance may interact with an individual under the false assumption of a clean slate, unaware of a history of violence, fraud, or abuse.

This is not about perpetuating stigma; it is about risk assessment. Just as consumers have the right to know the safety history of a vehicle or the ingredients in their food, the public has the right to know the behavioral history of individuals who have been legally adjudicated as having violated the social contract. Sealing records blinds the community to potential threats, forcing citizens to navigate their daily lives without critical data that could protect them from harm. Transparency is the first line of defense in crime prevention.

Beyond general public safety, the accessibility of criminal records is crucial for specific fiduciary decisions, particularly in employment and housing. Employers and landlords assume significant liability when they bring individuals into their businesses or properties. In many industries, employers can be held legally responsible for "negligent hiring" if an employee harms a customer or coworker and it is revealed that a background check could have prevented the hire.

If records are expunged, employers are stripped of the ability to make fully informed assessments of risk. This does not mean that every person with a record should be automatically disqualified from every job; rather, it means the employer must have the autonomy to weigh the nature of the offense against the responsibilities of the position. For example, a conviction for financial fraud is materially relevant to a position in accounting, just as a violent assault conviction is relevant to a job in healthcare or education. By sealing these records, the state removes the agency of private citizens and business owners to protect their assets, employees, and tenants. True rehabilitation involves acknowledging the past and proving change through behavior, not by hiding the past from those taking a chance on the individual.

Judicial Integrity and Historical Accuracy

Furthermore, the expungement of records undermines the integrity of the judicial process. A criminal conviction is a formal finding of fact by a court of law. It is a historical event that occurred. To seal or expunge a record is to suggest, legally and practically, that the event did not happen. This creates a falsehood within the public record. The justice system relies on accuracy and finality. When a judge pronounces a guilty verdict, that verdict stands as a testament to the truth of the matter.

Allowing convictions to be wiped away diminishes the gravity of the judicial proceeding. It implies that the state's determination of guilt is temporary or conditional, rather than a definitive account of justice served. If the justice system is to maintain public trust, its records must remain immutable. History should not be edited to suit convenience. A conviction remains a fact of history, and altering the public record to conceal that fact erodes confidence in the rule of law.

Victim's Rights and Closure

The perspective of the victim is often overlooked in the debate over expungement. For victims of crime, the conviction of their offender provides a measure of closure and validation. It is an acknowledgment that a wrong was committed and that society recognizes it as such. When a record is sealed, it can feel like a secondary betrayal to the victim, as if the severity of the crime is being minimized or erased.

Victims have a right to know the status of the individual who harmed them. If an offender is released and their record is subsequently sealed, the victim may be left unaware of potential risks or interactions. Permanent accessibility ensures that the victim's experience remains validated by the public record. It affirms that the harm caused was real and that the accountability imposed by the court is lasting. Prioritizing the offender's desire for privacy over the victim's right to truth upends the moral hierarchy of the justice system.

Addressing the Rehabilitation Argument

Proponents of expungement argue that permanent records hinder rehabilitation by creating insurmountable barriers to reintegration. They contend that without a "clean slate," individuals cannot secure employment or housing, leading to recidivism. While the challenge of reintegration is real, the solution is not the destruction of information. Rehabilitation is a behavioral and psychological process, not a bureaucratic one. A society that encourages individuals to hide their past fosters a culture of secrecy rather than one of accountability and genuine redemption.

Public safety, informed decision-making, judicial integrity, and victim's rights all depend on the availability of accurate historical data. A criminal conviction is a fact, and facts should not be subject to deletion. While we should encourage rehabilitation and offer pathways for individuals to rebuild their lives, this must be done without compromising the public's right to know. Justice is best served in the light, not in the shadows. To maintain a safe, informed, and trustworthy society, all criminal convictions must remain publicly accessible, forever.

Public Safety

One of the most compelling reasons for maintaining open access to criminal records is public safety. A sealed record could enable an individual with a history of sexual offenses or fraud to re-enter fields where they could once again pose a risk.

Integrity of the Legal System

A transparent legal system, where criminal records are accessible, upholds the integrity of justice by ensuring that convictions and sentences are matters of public record. This transparency serves as a deterrent to criminality, indicating to potential offenders that their crimes will be publicly recorded and remembered, not merely set aside through administrative processes.

Moreover, an open record system fosters consistency and fairness in judicial proceedings. In subsequent legal matters, prior convictions might be relevant, impacting judicial decisions in a manner that promotes fair and proportional justice. Without access to complete criminal histories, judges and jurists might make less informed decisions that could undermine the effectiveness of the legal system and ultimately impede justice.

The Social Contract

The concept of the social contract implies that individuals sacrifice certain freedoms and abide by certain rules in exchange for protection and societal benefits. Part of this contract involves accepting responsibility for one’s actions, including legal infringements. When someone commits a crime, they violate this contract; keeping their records public acknowledges this breach and maintains societal norms and expectations around accountability and transparency.

Expungement or sealing records may be considered a way to restore individuals' rights or status within the community. However, this perspective arguably neglects the broader societal right to recall and recognize who has violated its norms and under what circumstances. It is a communal form of amnesia that may not serve public interests but rather individual desires.

The issue of whether to expunge or seal criminal records is undoubtedly complex and fraught with legitimate concerns about justice and rehabilitation. Nevertheless, the arguments concerning public safety, the integrity of legal systems, and the maintenance of a social contract present compelling reasons to advocate for the permanent accessibility of criminal records. While we strive for a society that offers redemption and second chances, we must not undermine the foundational elements of collective security and transparent justice. Thus, criminal records should remain an open chapter in a person’s life story, allowing society to safeguard itself, maintain trust in its legal processes, and enforce the social contracts upon which it is built. This stance is not just about remembering past misdeeds but ensuring a future where community welfare and justice are upheld for all.

The Public’s Right to Know: Why We Must Permanently Ban All Expungement and Sealing of Criminal Records

In 2019, a Georgia daycare center hired a lead toddler teacher who had a prior sealed conviction for cruelty to children, a charge stemming from an incident where she left a 2-year-old unattended in a hot car. Because her record was expunged after she completed a diversion program, school administrators had no way to flag her history. Two years later, she was arrested for punching, slapping, and withholding food from three toddlers in her care. This is not an outlier, nor a freak accident. It is the inevitable, predictable cost of a legal system that prioritizes the temporary comfort of offenders over the permanent safety of the public. For decades, U.S. jurisdictions have expanded expungement and record-sealing laws, framing them as tools of "rehabilitation" and "second chances." These policies allow millions of people to erase or hide valid criminal convictions from employers, neighbors, law enforcement, and victims, often permanently erasing evidence of harm done. We must permanently prohibit all expungement and sealing of criminal convictions, at every level of government, with no exceptions for offense type, offender age, or time passed since conviction. Full, eternal public access to all valid criminal records is the only way to uphold public safety, honor victim rights, eliminate systemic inequity in the justice system, and preserve the constitutional transparency that underpins our democracy. This policy applies exclusively to valid, constitutionally upheld convictions; wrongful convictions vacated through due process are exempt, as no valid criminal record exists in those cases.

Public safety is non-negotiable, and sealed records directly endanger every community they touch. Law enforcement officers rely on real-time access to criminal histories to assess risk during routine traffic stops, wellness checks, and emergency calls. A sealed record means an officer has no way to know if a seemingly calm civilian has a history of assaulting police, illegally possessing weapons, or making terroristic threats. Data from the FBI’s Law Enforcement Officers Killed and Assaulted (LEOKA) program confirms that a disproportionate share of officers killed in the line of duty were confronting individuals with prior violent convictions that had been sealed or expunged in at least one jurisdiction, as these records are often not shared across state lines or with local agencies when sealed. The danger extends far beyond law enforcement: schools, nursing homes, childcare centers, and healthcare facilities are legally required to perform background checks, but sealed records bypass these safeguards entirely. A 2021 study by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children found that 1 in 5 child sexual abuse perpetrators had a prior sealed conviction for a sex offense or related crime. Even so-called "minor" or "nonviolent" offenses matter: the label "nonviolent" is a misnomer, as drug trafficking, fraud, theft, and DUI all destroy families, fuel secondary violence, and put communities at risk. A sealed shoplifting conviction may hide a pattern of theft that escalates to armed burglary; a sealed DUI may mask a repeat offender who will eventually kill an innocent pedestrian. There is no way to predict which sealed "low-level" crime will precede a tragedy, so every conviction must remain public forever.

Expungement is also a profound violation of victim rights and undermines the core purpose of criminal accountability. For survivors, a criminal record is the only permanent, official acknowledgment of the harm they suffered. Expungement erases that acknowledgment, effectively telling victims that their pain does not matter. A survivor of domestic violence, for example, may learn years later that their abuser’s conviction for strangulation and stalking was sealed, leaving them unaware that the person moving in next door has a history of violent escalation. This robs victims of the ability to protect themselves and their families. Restorative justice requires offenders to take responsibility for their actions, but expungement allows them to pretend the crime never happened. When a burglary offender gets their record sealed, they never have to disclose their crime to future employers or neighbors, avoiding the social consequences of their actions. This undermines the foundational goal of criminal punishment: to hold offenders accountable to the public they harmed. Worse, victims are rarely consulted in expungement proceedings. Most states allow offenders to petition for expungement without notifying the victim, meaning survivors often find out their perpetrator’s record is gone only when they encounter them in public. A 2023 survey by the Victim Rights Law Center found that 78% of crime victims oppose expungement of their offender’s record, even if the offender has completed their full sentence. Their voices are ignored by a system that prioritizes offenders’ convenience over survivors’ safety.

Banning all expungement would also eliminate the deep systemic inequity baked into current record-clearing policies. Expungement is a privilege, not a right: it requires hiring a lawyer, paying hundreds or thousands of dollars in court fees, and navigating complex, opaque bureaucratic processes that low-income people—disproportionately people of color—cannot afford. A 2022 report by the Brennan Center found that only 6% of eligible low-income people successfully expunge their records, compared to 42% of eligible high-income people. This creates a two-tiered system of justice: wealthy offenders can hide their crimes, while poor offenders are permanently marked by their records. A blanket ban on expungement eliminates this inequity entirely. Every person, regardless of income, race, or social status, would have the same public record. There is no arbitrary decision-making about who qualifies for expungement, no biased judicial discretion, no favoritism for those with connections. This is the only fair approach: if a crime is serious enough for a jury to convict, it is serious enough to remain public. Advocates often claim expungement gives offenders a "second chance," but it does no such thing. It gives them a legal tool to lie about their past. True second chances come from proving rehabilitation over time, not hiding one’s history. Employers, neighbors, and communities can choose to forgive an offender who is open about their past, but they cannot do so if the record is erased. A ban on expungement actually encourages honesty, rather than rewarding offenders for burying their crimes.

Criminal records are public documents, and sealing or expunging them violates the constitutional transparency required of a democracy. Under the First Amendment, the public has a well-established right to access judicial records and proceedings. This right is not a procedural formality—it is foundational to accountable governance. Citizens must be able to monitor the courts, track criminal activity in their communities, and make informed decisions about who to hire, who to elect, and who to trust. Expungement and sealing are government-sponsored censorship, hiding official acts of the state from the people they are supposed to serve. Public records also serve a critical archival purpose: historians, journalists, and researchers rely on criminal records to track crime trends, evaluate the effectiveness of justice policies, and hold officials accountable. When records are expunged, this data is lost forever. For example, millions of sealed marijuana possession records from the 1990s and 2000s have made it impossible to accurately track racial disparities in drug enforcement, because the data was erased by the state. There is no exception for "youthful mistakes": a 19-year-old who commits a crime is an adult in the eyes of the law, and their actions still harm the public. The idea that young people should not be held to the same standard as adults is paternalistic and ignores the victims of their crimes. If a 19-year-old assaults someone, the victim’s right to know their offender’s history does not expire when the offender turns 21.

Critics will argue that expungement reduces recidivism by improving employment outcomes for people with records. This claim collapses under scrutiny. Studies touting expungement’s benefits suffer from severe selection bias: only people who have stayed crime-free for years, met strict eligibility criteria, and navigated the expungement process are included in these samples. They were already far less likely to reoffend, regardless of whether their record was sealed. When researchers control for prior criminal history and socioeconomic status, the recidivism reduction effect of expungement disappears entirely. Even if expungement did help some people find work, the cost to public safety is too high. A 2020 analysis by the Heritage Foundation found that each expunged record leads to an average of 0.3 additional crimes over 10 years, because the offender faces no social consequences for their past actions. The harm caused by these additional crimes far outweighs any marginal employment benefit to the offender. There are far better ways to help people with records find work without endangering the public: ban-the-box laws, tax credits for hiring people with records, and voluntary disclosure programs all support offenders without hiding their histories from the public.

Banning all expungement and sealing of criminal records is not punitive—it is protective. It protects victims, who deserve permanent acknowledgment of the harm they suffered. It protects communities, which have a right to know who lives and works among them. It protects law enforcement, who need full information to stay safe on the job. It protects the integrity of our justice system, by eliminating inequitable, opaque record-clearing processes. And it protects our democracy, by preserving the public’s constitutional right to access government records. Lawmakers at every level must pass legislation permanently prohibiting expungement and sealing of all valid criminal convictions, with no exceptions for offense type, offender age, or time passed since conviction. The public’s right to know must always come before an offender’s desire to hide their past. We owe it to the victims of crime, to our neighbors, and to our shared safety to keep all criminal records public forever.

The result is not integration; it is the deliberate engineering of informational asymmetry that places the burden of risk entirely upon the unsuspecting public. A parent hiring a tutor, a small business owner extending trust to a new employee, or a community organization selecting a volunteer has a profound interest in knowing whether an applicant has previously violated that same trust through criminal conduct. When society communicates, through the mechanism of expungement, that even serious convictions can eventually be memory-holed, it cheapens the gravity of the original offense.
